A CFC is a foreign resident company where a control test is satisfied (see below). 
First criteria: whether the CFC is a resident of a listed (Canada, France, Germany, Japan, NZ, UK, US) or unlisted country (all other countries). 
Second criteria: one of the three control tests must be satisfied. In particular: 
- Strict control: a group of five or fewer Australian 1 per cent entities and their associates hold at least 50 per cent (direct and indirect interests) of the foreign company. 
- Assumed control: a foreign company owns or is entitled to acquire an associate-inclusive control interest of at least 40 per cent in the foreign company. 
- De facto control: a group of five or fewer Australian entities, either alone or with associates, effectively controls the foreign company.

A foreign company will be considered as a CFC if the following two conditions are simultaneously satisfied:     - The control test: the Belgian taxpayer owns with or without its associated entities the majority of the voting rights attached to the total of the shares of the foreign company, or holds together with its associated entities a stake of at least 50% in the capital of this company, or is together with its associated entities entitled to at least 50% of the profits of this company; and     - The taxation test: in the country or jurisdiction where it is situated, the foreign company/PE is either not subject to income tax or subject to income tax less than half of the income tax if the company/PE would have been located in Belgium.

There are no general exemptions based on whether the CFC is undertaking substantial activities. However, there are substance-based exceptions from certain specific rules in Canada's CFC regime that otherwise include a CFC's active business income in its CFC income. Very generally, if a CFC carries on an active business the principal purpose of which is to earn income that is of a type that is generally passive in nature (e.g., interest or royalty income), then the income is subject to the CFC rule, unless among other requirements the CFC carries on the business principally with arm's length persons and it employs more than five full-time employees in the active conduct of the business. There are also exceptions from the "base erosion" rules, which exceptions generally apply where more than 90 percent of the CFC's gross revenues from the specific activity to which a given base erosion rule applies (e.g., the lending of money to Canadian residents) derives from transactions with arm's length non-residents.

Generally, a CFC is a "foreign affiliate" that is legally controlled by the Canadian shareholder, or that would be controlled by the shareholder if the shareholder owned all of the shares of the foreign corporation that are owned by the taxpayer, persons that do not deal at arm's length with the taxpayer, and any other four Canadian residents. A "foreign affiliate" of a Canadian taxpayer is a non-resident corporation, where at least 1 percent of the shares of any class are owned, directly or indirectly, by the Canadian shareholder and at least 10 percent of the shares of any class are owned, directly or indirectly, by the Canadian shareholder together with related persons.

Control test criteria consider a foreign entity to be controlled if residents of Chile have:     - 50% or more of the foreign entity's capital, profits or voting power;     - the power to elect the majority of directors or administrators of the foreign entity; or     - the power to unilaterally amend the foreign entity's by laws, or to change the majority of its directors or administrators.        A foreign entity is deemed to be a CFC if:     - it is resident in a low-tax jurisdiction as defined in article 41H of the Income Tax Law; or     - a person resident of Chile has directly or indirectly a purchase option with respect to the foreign entity for 50% or more of its capital, profits or voting power.

An arrangement or a series thereof shall be regarded as non-genuine to the extent that the entity or permanent establishment would not own the assets or would not have undertaken the risks which generate all, or part of, its income if it were not controlled by a company where the significant people functions, which are relevant to those assets and risks, are carried out and are instrumental in generating the controlled company's income.        In case of CFC rule applicable to natural persons, there is an exemption for a CFC if more than 50 per cent of its annual income is derived from actual economic activity or if the state or territory of location of the legal person provides the Estonian tax authority with information concerning the income of a person controlled by Estonian residents.

As of January 1, 2019, there are two CFC rules in Estonia:        1) CFC rule from the ATAD Directive applicable to companies;    2) CFC rule applicable to natural persons. In case of CFC rule applicable to natural persons, a legal person is deemed to be controlled by Estonian residents if one or several legal or natural persons who are Estonian residents own at least 50 per cent of the shares, votes or rights to the profits of the legal person directly or together with associated persons.        The income of a foreign legal person is deemed to be the taxable income of a resident natural person if the condition prescribed above is fulfilled and the resident owns at least 10 per cent of the shares, votes or rights to the profits of the legal person directly or together with associated persons.

The CFC rules requires, under some circumstances, the taxation in France, in the hands of a French corporation, of the profits of a foreign entity which it owns.                                                          There are both control and low taxation threshold requirements :     - a French corporation falls within the scope of CFC if it owns directly or indirectly more than 50 per cent of the share or voting rights of a foreign entity (company, subsidiary, branches, trust or comparable entities) ;  This threshold is reduced to 5% when more than 50% of the shares, shares, financial rights or voting rights of the legal entity established or incorporated outside France are held by companies established in France which act in concert, when the foreign entity is listed on a regulated market, or by companies that are directly or indirectly placed in a situation of control or dependence with respect to the legal person established in France and the foreign entity benefits from a preferential tax regime in the foreign State. An entity is considered to benefit from a preferential tax regime if it is not taxable in that State or taxable at a level that is less than 40% or more than it would have paid under the french law if it had been located in France (the threshold of 40 % applies from the 1st of January 2020, before that date the 50 % threshold applies).

CFC rules, in principle, are not applicable with respect of foreign branches or subsidiaries located in another EU country. However, this exception is not applicable if the French tax authorities can demonstrate that the foreign entity located in another EU country constitutes an artificial arrangement, set up to circumvent French tax legislation. This concept is similar to the ‘abuse of law’ concept, although it does not have all the same characteristics.
In other cases, if a French company falls within the scope of CFC, it can be exempt if it demonstrates that the operations of the entity established outside France are primarily intended to have an object and effect other than to transfer profits in a State or territory where it is subject to a preferential tax regime.                         This condition is deemed to be fulfilled when the entity established outside France has mainly an industrial or commercial activity.

There are two series of exemptions :                                               - Inside the EU, the foreign entity established in a member State will not be subject to the CFC rules, unless  the French tax authorities demonstrate that the foreign entity located in another EU country constitutes an artificial arrangement, set up to circumvent French tax legislation ;                                                   - In other cases, if a French company falls within the scope of CFC, it can be exempt if it demonstrates that the operations of the entity established outside France are primarily intended to have an object and effect other than to transfer profits in a State or territory where it is subject to a preferential tax regime. According to par.1 of article 66 of Income Tax Code (ITC), a CFC is a foreign legal person, or foreign legal entity, or a foreign permanent establishment of which the profits are not subject to tax or are exempt from tax, if the following conditions are met cumulatively: 
a) in the case of an entity, the taxpayer by itself, or together with its associated enterprises holds a direct or indirect participation of more than 50 percent of the voting rights, or owns directly or indirectly more than 50 percent of capital or is entitled to receive more than 50 percent of the profits of that entity; and
b) the actual corporate tax paid on its profits by the entity or permanent establishment is lower than the difference between the corporate tax that would have been charged on the entity or permanent establishment under the Greek corporate tax system of the taxpayer that would be due by such person in Greece and the actual corporate tax paid on its profits by the entity or permanent establishment; and
c) if more than thirty percent (30%) of net income before tax realized by the legal person or legal entity falls into one or more certain categories as defined in paragraph 3 of the same article (ITC). 

A CFC is a legal person or entity which is resident for tax purposes in another country if the following conditions are met cumulatively:    a) if the taxpayer alone or jointly with the associated persons directly or indirectly holds shares, stakes, voting rights or participations in the capital exceeding fifty percent (50%) or is entitled to over fifty percent (50%) of the profit of that legal person or entity,    b) if the above legal person or entity is subject to taxation in a non-cooperating state or a country with a preferential tax regime, i.e. a special regime allowing for a substantially lower taxation level than that under the general regime,    c) if more than thirty percent (30%) of net income before tax realized by the legal person or entity falls into one or more certain categories defined in the very same article,    d) the legal person or entity is not a company of which the main class of shares of which are traded on a regulated market.

Section 835I defines "chargeable income" as meaning 'the undistributed income of a controlled foreign company which is subject to a controlled foreign company charge'. Undistributed income means the distributable profits for the accounting period of a CFC less any relevant distribution. The full definition is set out in section 835Q.  Under section 835R, the amount of undistributed income that the CFC charge can arise on is the portion included in the accounting profits of the company available for distribution that is attributable to the relevant Irish activities i.e. Irish SPFs, where those SPFs were instrumental in generating the income and the arrangements involving the SPFs were non-genuine (i.e. the CFC would not have owned the assets nor borne the risks that it did were it not for the Irish SPFs). A CFC charge will therefore arise if those arrangements were non-genuine and were put in place for the essential purpose of avoiding tax..

The exemptions that apply include scenarios where the CFC pays a comparatively higher amount of tax in its territory than it would have paid in the State (section 835T Effective tax rate exemption), the low profit margin exemption (section 835U), the low accounting profit exemption (section 835V) and the exempt period exemption (section 835W).  The CFC rules will not apply where the arrangements, under which SPFs are performed, have been entered into on an arm’s length basis or are subject to the Transfer Pricing regime under Part 35A, TCA (section 835R).

The CFC rules are an anti-abuse measure, designed to prevent the artificial diversion of profits from controlling companies to offshore entities in low or no-tax jurisdictions (the CFCs). The rules operate by attributing undistributed income of the CFCs, arising from non-genuine arrangements put in place for the essential purpose of avoiding tax, to the controlling company, or a connected company in the State for taxation, where the controlling company, or a connected company, carry out relevant Irish activities (i.e. significant people functions (SPFs) or key entrepreneurial risk-taking functions (KERTs) in the State). In that regard, the CFC rules focus less on substance in the CFC and focus more on what activity is being carried out on its behalf in the controlling company.  The rules require an analysis as to the extent to which the CFC would hold assets or bear risks were it not for the controlling company, or a connected company, undertaking the SPFs or KERTs in relation to those assets and risks.

A controlled foreign taxable subject (i.e. CFC) means:    1) a controlled foreign taxable entity;    2) a permanent establishment of a Lithuanian entity whose income is not attributable to the tax base of the Lithuanian entity.        A controlled foreign taxable entity means a foreign entity where a Lithuanian entity alone or together with associated persons on the last date of the tax period of this foreign entity directly or indirectly owns more than 50 % of shares (interests, member shares), voting rights or rights to the share of distributable profits or exclusive rights to purchase them.        The income of the CFC is taxed only if:    1) a CFC is registered or otherwise organised in the target territory (blacklisted jurisdiction); or    2) passive income of the CFC exceeds 1/3 of total income of this CFC during the tax period; and    3) an actual corporate tax of the CFC calculated of the income of that CFC according to the rules of corporate tax or similar tax applicable in that foreign state is lower than 50 per cent of an actual corporate tax which would have been calculated of the income of that CFC according to the provisions of  Law on Corporate Income Tax. For the purposes of this item, no account shall be taken of the income that has been earned by the CFC through a permanent establishment in another foreign state which is not taxed in a foreign state where the CFC is registered or otherwise organised.  For the purpose of this paragraph, CFC income includes only passive income.

CFC rules are not applied if (except for the CFC, registered or otherwise organised in the target territory (blacklisted jurisdictions)):- passive income of the CFC does not exceed 1/3 of total income of this CFC during the tax period; or- actual corporate income tax paid on income of the CFC following the rules on corporate income tax or equivalent tax applied in this foreign state is not lower than 50 % of actual corporate income tax on income of CFC which would have been computed following the Lithuanian CFC rules.

CFC rules are not applied in cases when CFC (except for the CFC, registered or otherwise organised in the target territory (blacklisted jurisdictions)) has staff members and uses assets to ensure actual economic activities in the jurisdiction where this CFC is registered or otherwise organised.

(II) countries with which Poland/EU have not ratified any treaty (e.g. DTTs) allowing for exchange of tax information 
No other conditions have to be met in these cases for the foreign entity to be considered as a CFC.
In addition, a controlled foreign company (III) will be an entity that meets all of the following conditions:
the control level condition - Polish tax residents have directly/indirectly, solely or jointly with related entities or with non-related entities being Polish tax residents, over 50% participation in the foreign company’s income, voting rights, or capital or exercise actual control over the foreign entity.
the level of taxation condition - Income tax actually paid by the foreign entity (not subject to refund or credit in any form, including the refund or credit for the benefit of another entity) is lower by at least 25% than the income tax that would be paid by this foreign company in Poland at the application of the 19% tax rate (if it was a Polish tax resident)
the revenue structure condition – at least 33% of the revenue of this entity earned in the tax year comes from the indicated sources (so-called passive income)
As of 2022. there are also 2 more categories of CFC entities regarding so-called "shell companies”
The first is entities (IV) that, in addition to meeting the level of control and the level of taxation conditions, have assets that generate passive income with a value equivalent to at least 50% of the value of the entity's total assets, and the passive income is less than 30% of the value of assets and receivables.
The last category of CFC (V) entities are those defined by reference to the rate of return on assets held. A foreign entity will be considered a CFC if, in addition to the level of control condition and the level of taxation condition, it earns income in excess of the income calculated according to the formula: (b + c + d) × 20%, in which the various letters stand for: b - the carrying value of the entity's assets, c - the entity's annual employment costs, d - the accumulated (summed) previous depreciation and amortization within the meaning of the accounting regulations, and less than 75% of the entity's income is derived from transactions with unrelated parties domiciled, established, managed, registered or located in the same country as the entity.

Portuguese definition of CFC (see article 66, CITC): Profits or incomes of non-residents in Portugal and submitted to clearly more favourable tax regime are treated (with appropriate deductions) as profits or incomes of companies with residence in Portugal that, directly or indirectly, have at least 25% of capital, voting rights, rights on profits or incomes or rights on assets of said non-residents companies. A non-resident company is considered submitted to a clearly more favourable tax regime if the residence jurisdiction is by law considered has such or if that company pays an effective CIT or equivalent lower than 50% of the Portuguese one.

Other condition, which has to be fulfilled is a tax rate test, i.e. the corporate tax paid by the controlled foreign company abroad is lower than the difference between the corporate tax of the controlled foreign company calculated under the Slovak Income Tax Act and the corporate tax paid by the controlled foreign company abroad [ITA Sec. 17h para 1 letter b)].    As the controlled foreign company is considered also the permanent establishment [ITA Sec. 17h para 3].

However, income is not considered to be subject to low taxation if the foreign legal entity is a tax resident, and liable to income tax, in one of the countries listed in a white list, provided that the income in question has not been expressly excluded in the list. A foreign company is a CFC when UK persons, together with related persons in the UK or elsewhere,  hold more than a 50% interest in that company, by reference to legal control, economic control, or accounting standards. A separate test applies to joint ventures. CFC income is computed on basis of UK corporate tax rules, with separate charging provisions for trading income, non-trade finance profits and trading finance profits.

The SPF approach in relation to trading profits and non-trade finance profits effectively applies a test of substance or relevant activity at an asset or risk level, which can be seen as a measure of relevant economic susbtance and activity. In addition, the rules apply a business premises condition in relation to trading profits and intra-group non-trading finance profits, which have to be occupied with a degree of permanence and from where the business of the CFC has to be carried on. For completeness, other exemptions include : Tax rate exemption - where the local tax paid is at least 75% of the tax that would have been paid in the UK.    De minimis threshold - less than £50k profits in a 12 month period, or less than £500k profits so long as passive interest income does not exceed £50k in that period.    Low profit margin exemption - where accounting profits are not more than 10% of relevant operating expenses.    Excluded countries list based on regimes with similar tax rules to UK, subject to an anti-avoidance test and limits on passive income.    Temporary exemption period for certain acquisitions, subject to anti-avoidance conditions.    Partial and full exemption for certain types of intra-group finance profits, subject to detailed anti-avoidance conditions.    Exemption for certain trading profits where a minority of significant people functions are carried out in the UK.

The UK rules in relation to trading profits operate by reference to where the significant people functions (SPFs) that generate those profits are carried out, rather than by applying a generic test in relation to substantial activities. Broadly speaking, a CFC charge arises  in respect on any trading profits where the majority of the SPFs which generate those profits are carried out in the UK. For trading finance profits (banking and insurance) a charge will arise where the CFC is overcapitalised with funds received from UK connected persons (UK group companies). For non-trade finance profits, a charge will arise in relation to funds generated by UK SPFs, funds generated by UK connected capital (from UK group companies), arrangements in lieu of dividends to the UK and certain leasing arrangements. For certain intra-group financing arrangements, a partial (75%) exemption can be applied and, in limited circumstances, a full (100%) exemption can apply. Other entity level exemptions can apply in relatio to low profits, low profit margins, high effective tax rates (at least 75% of UK corporation ETR) and excluded countries with similar tax base/rate to UK.

The United States has two sets of CFC inclusion rules.  A U.S. shareholder must include in income their share of the subpart F income (generally, passive/mobile income) of a CFC.  The subpart F income rules include a   de minimis rule   - income that would otherwise be subpart F income is not treated as subpart F income if it is less than the lesser of 5% of the CFC’s gross income or USD $1,000,000.  However, all of a CFC’s income will be treated as subpart F income if the CFC’s subpart F income and insurance income exceeds 70% of the CFC’s gross income.  The subpart F income rules also include a high tax exception – subpart F income that is subject to an effective rate of income tax imposed by a foreign country greater than 90% of the maximum rate of U.S. tax imposed on corporations (currently, greater than 18.9%).  The second set of rules (adopted in 2017) requires a U.S. shareholder to include in income their global intangible low-taxed income (GILTI).  The GILTI rules apply a formulaic approach which generally requires an income inclusion by the U.S. shareholder based on their share of the income of their CFCs after excluding a 10% return on tangible assets of the CFCs from the GILTI amount.  Such income also excludes income that is effectively connected to a trade or business in the United States (which is taxed separately), subpart F income, related-party dividends, foreign oil and gas extraction income, or income that would be subpart F but is excluded by the high-tax exception.  In addition, the GILTI regime has an exclusion for high-taxed income, pursuant to an election, similar to the high tax exception for the Subpart F rules.

A U.S. shareholder is defined as a United States person (U.S. person) who owns 10 percent or more of the vote or value of all classes of stock of a corporation. A foreign company will be considered as a CFC if the following two conditions are simultaneously satisfied:    
 - The control test: the Belgian taxpayer owns with or without its associated entities the majority of the voting rights attached to the total of the shares of the foreign company, or holds together with its associated entities a stake of at least 50% in the capital of this company, or is together with its associated entities entitled to at least 50% of the profits of this company; and     
- The taxation test: in the country or jurisdiction where it is situated, the foreign company/PE is either not subject to income tax or subject to income tax less than half of the income tax if the company/PE would have been located in Belgium.

Both a relative and a fixed rate mechanism are applied.
According to article 185/2, § 3, BITC 92, Belgium applies a “low taxation” test with a default relative trigger. It states that foreign entities (PEs or companies) are low-taxed if the foreign income tax is below half of the “theoretical Belgian CIT” (Belgian corporate income tax that would be due if it were established in Belgium and computed under Belgian rules — excluding profits attributable to the foreign entity’s own treaty-exempt PEs). Belgium’s standard nominal CIT rate is 25%, so, for example, the low tax test is satisfied if the foreign income tax is below 12,5% when the theoretical Belgian CIT would be 25%. More generally, the relative trigger equals half of the Belgian-theory rate (e.g., 22% ⇒ 11%).
However, where such foreign entities are established in a non-EEA jurisdiction, the “relative” trigger effectively has a floor because the low-tax condition is deemed satisfied (rebuttable presumption) under the “low or no tax jurisdiction” rule in article 307, § 1/2, BITC 92, which identifies such jurisdictions inter alia by a nominal CIT below 10%. In the same cases, there is also a criterion based on an effective tax on foreign-source income below 15%. In practice, these 10%/15% thresholds operate as fixed reference points for the low-rate assessment of non-EEA jurisdictions.
Besides, the administration clarified in Circular 2024/C/82 (on CFC rules) that a (Q)DMTT collected abroad is not treated as an “income tax” for the CFC low-tax test (i.e., it is ignored when assessing the low-tax condition)."

CFC income is defined as "foreign accrual property income" (FAPI) under the Canadian Income Tax Act (Act). In the most general terms, FAPI includes income from property such as interest, dividends, rents, royalties or any similar returns or substitutes (as well as income from singular ventures). Capital gains from the disposition of non-"excluded property" i.e. property not connected to an active business are also included.  FAPI income is computed by applying the Act as if the CFA were a resident of Canada.

More specifically:
• FAPI includes income from property as well as income from an "investment business" (i.e. a business whose principal purpose is to earn income from property sources and other specifically enumerated types of passive income). Unless one of the exceptions to investment business are met (please refer to our responses to Q1.7 in column G), income derived from property, the insurance or reinsurance of risk, the factoring of trade accounts receivable, or the disposition of "investment property" is included in FAPI.

• Excluded property generally refers to property used principally in carrying on active business. It also includes foreign affiliate shares of which more than 90% of the value is attributable to active business assets.

• Income from a "non-qualifying business" is also FAPI.  Non-qualifying business generally refers to active business carried on in a non-qualifying country. In general terms,  a country is a non-qualifying country if it has not entered into a tax convention or a tax information exchange agreement with Canada within 5 years after being invited to do so.

• The Canadian CFC rules contain an extensive set of other provisions that apply for the purpose of determining FAPI. For example, there are rules that (1)  recharacterize certain property income as active business income, (2) recharacterize as FAPI certain otherwise active business income that is considered to be base-eroding, (3) provide rollovers for reorganizational transactions, and (4) deem certain gains and losses to be nil.

Generally, a CFC is a "foreign affiliate" that is legally controlled by the Canadian shareholder, or that would be controlled by the shareholder if the shareholder owned all of the shares of the foreign corporation that are owned by the taxpayer, persons that do not deal at arm's length with the taxpayer, and any other four Canadian residents. The CFC rules are an anti-abuse measure, designed to prevent the artificial diversion of profits from controlling companies to offshore entities in low or no-tax jurisdictions (the CFCs). 
The rules operate by attributing undistributed income of the CFCs, arising from non-genuine arrangements put in place for the essential purpose of avoiding tax,
to the controlling company, or a connected company in the State for taxation, 
where the controlling company, or a connected company, carry out relevant Irish activities 
(i.e. significant people functions (SPFs) or 
key entrepreneurial risk-taking functions (KERTs) in the State). 
In that regard, the CFC rules focus less on substance in the CFC and focus more on what activity is being carried out on its behalf in the controlling company. 
The rules require an analysis as to the extent to which the CFC would hold assets or bear risks were it not for the controlling company, or a connected company, undertaking the SPFs or KERTs in relation to those assets and risks.

Section 835I defines "chargeable income" as meaning 'the undistributed income of a controlled foreign company which is subject to a controlled foreign company charge'. 
Undistributed income means the distributable profits for the accounting period of a CFC less any relevant distribution. The full definition is set out in section 835Q. 
Under section 835R, the amount of undistributed income that the CFC charge can arise on is the portion included in the accounting profits of the company available for distribution that is attributable to the relevant Irish activities 
i.e. Irish Significant People Functions (SPF) or Key Entrepreneurial risk taking functions (KERTs), where those SPFs (taken to include KERT's) were instrumental in generating the income and
 the arrangements involving the SPFs were non-genuine (i.e. the CFC would not have owned the assets nor borne the risks that it did were it not for the Irish SPFs). 
A CFC charge will therefore arise if those arrangements were non-genuine and were put in place for the essential purpose of avoiding tax.
The definition of accounting profits in section 835I, means the amount of profit, before taxation, shown in the profit and loss account, without regard to any capital gains and losses, dividends or distributions which would be exempt from tax in determining the CFC’s corresponding chargeable profits in Ireland.

With respect to the substantial requirements, we have the concept of the Specified CFCs and the Economic Activity Tests as described below.

1. Specified CFCs
The basic idea of the Specified CFCs is that a CFC having no substance and apparently earning only passive income is generally subject to the CFC rules. The Specified CFCs consists of following 3 types of CFC.

(1) Paper company
A Paper company  is a CFC that meets neither of the following conditions:
Substance Test: The CFC maintains an office, store, factory or other fixed place of business necessary to conduct its business . and
Administration  and control test: The CFC functions with its own administration, control and management in the country in which the head office of the subsidiary is located .

(2) Cash box  
Cash box is a CFC that falls under either (a) or (b).
(a) CFC that meets both of the following requirements;
Passive Income Test: the ratio of the passive income to the total amounts of its gross assets exceed 30%; and
Asset Test: the ratio of the amount of securities, loan receivables, tangible assets for leasing and intangible assets exceed 50% of the total amount of its gross assets .
or
(b) CFC that meets both of the following requirements;
Insurance Income Test: the ratio of the total insurance income from non-related parties to the total insurance income is less than  10%; and
Insurance Payment Test: the ratio of the total reinsurance payment to non-related parties to the total insurance income from related parties (insurance income other than insurance income from non-related parties) is less than  50%.

(3) Blacklist company
A Blacklist company is a CFC that has a head or principal office in the jurisdiction designated by the Minister of Finance as a non-cooperative jurisdiction with respect to the exchange of information for tax purposes.

2. Economic Activity Tests
Economic Activity Tests consists of following requirements.
CFC that meets any of the requirements below is categorized into the Partial inclusion CFC and only passive income of such CFC is subject to the CFC rules.
(1) Primary business test
The primary business of a CFC is not any of the following businesses:
・Holding of shares and bonds
・Licensing of intangibles
・Leasing of vessels or aircraft
(2) Substance test
The CFC maintains an office, store, factory or other fixed place of business necessary to conduct its business in the country where the head office of the subsidiary is located.
(3) Administration and control test
The CFC functions with its own administration, control and management in the country where the head office of the subsidiary is located
(4)-a Unrelated Party Test
The CFC conducts its business mainly (more than 50%) with unrelated parties.
(4)-b Country of location test
The CFC conducts its business mainly in the country in which the head office of the subsidiary is located.

The Korean resident holding directly or indirectly 10% or more of shares in such company(including the direct holdings by the specially-related persons) is subject to CFC rules.    2. The foreign company is located in a significantly low tax jurisdiction with an average effective tax rate of 15% or less on taxable income for the past three years.

The CFC rule is not applicable to an entity or permanent establishment with accounting profits of no more than EUR 750 000, and non-trading income of no more than EUR 75 000. However, this exclusion is not applicable for entity set or established in a low tax or no tax countries and territories.

The CFC is defined as a permanent establishment or an entity if the taxpayer by itself, or together with its associated enterprises holds a direct or indirect participation of more than 50 percent of the voting rights, or owns directly or indirectly more than 50 percent of capital or is entitled to receive more than 50 percent of the profits of that entity.

CFC rules apply if the CFC’s income arises from non-genuine arrangements that have been put in place with the essential purpose of obtaining a tax advantage (as provided in Article 7(2)(b) of the ATAD).
At the same time, this provision does not apply to CFCs whose accounting profits do not exceed EUR 750,000 and whose non-trading income does not exceed EUR 75,000, and which are not established in low-tax or tax-free jurisdictions as defined in national legislation.
Therefore, we do not assess the actual corporate tax paid by the CFC on its profits, nor do we track the income by specific categories.

In other words, under our law implementing ATAD CFC regulation a taxpayer shall include in their taxable base the part of the CFC profits (increase in asset value) which has been obtained from non-genuine arrangements of CFC`s. To avoid any double taxation, the taxpayer is entitled to adjust its tax base in amount of received dividends from CFC`s which was prior included.

Latvia do not apply trigger rate.
A taxpayer shall include in their taxable base the part of the CFC profits (increase in asset value) which has been obtained from non-genuine arrangements of CFC`s and the corporate income tax rate is 20% (20/80) applicable to the taxable base. To avoid any double taxation, the taxpayer is entitled to adjust its tax base in amount of received dividends from CFC`s which was prior included.

CFC rules are not applied in cases when CFC (except for the CFC, registered or otherwise organised in the target territory (blacklisted jurisdictions)) has staff members and uses assets to ensure actual economic activities in the jurisdiction where this CFC is registered or otherwise organised.

CFC rules are not applied if (except for the CFC, registered or otherwise organised in the target territory (blacklisted jurisdictions)):- passive income of the CFC does not exceed 1/3 of total income of this CFC during the tax period; or- actual corporate income tax paid on income of the CFC following the rules on corporate income tax or equivalent tax applied in this foreign state is not lower than 50 % of actual corporate income tax on income of CFC which would have been computed following the Lithuanian CFC rules.

A controlled foreign taxable subject (i.e. CFC) means:    1) a controlled foreign taxable entity;    2) a permanent establishment of a Lithuanian entity whose income is not attributable to the tax base of the Lithuanian entity.        A controlled foreign taxable entity means a foreign entity where a Lithuanian entity alone or together with associated persons on the last date of the tax period of this foreign entity directly or indirectly owns more than 50 % of shares (interests, member shares), voting rights or rights to the share of distributable profits or exclusive rights to purchase them.        The income of the CFC is taxed only if:    1) a CFC is registered or otherwise organised in the target territory (blacklisted jurisdiction); or    2) passive income of the CFC exceeds 1/3 of total income of this CFC during the tax period; and    3) an actual corporate tax of the CFC calculated of the income of that CFC according to the rules of corporate tax or similar tax applicable in that foreign state is lower than 50 per cent of an actual corporate tax which would have been calculated of the income of that CFC according to the provisions of  Law on Corporate Income Tax. For the purposes of this item, no account shall be taken of the income that has been earned by the CFC through a permanent establishment in another foreign state which is not taxed in a foreign state where the CFC is registered or otherwise organised.  For the purpose of this paragraph, CFC income includes only passive income.

Under Luxembourg tax law, a CFC is a foreign entity or permanent establishment (PE) whose profits are not subject to tax or are exempt in Luxembourg, in which a Luxembourg taxpayer, alone or together with associated enterprises, holds directly or indirectly more than 50% of the voting rights, capital ownership, or entitlement to profits of the entity (control test), and whose income is subject to an effective tax rate that is less than 50% of the Luxembourg tax that would have been due on the same income (low-taxation condition). Pursuant to Article 164ter of the Luxembourg Income Tax Law (LITL), the non-distributed income of the CFC that arises from non-genuine arrangements put in place essentially to obtain a tax advantage is attributed to the Luxembourg controlling taxpayer.

Beyond the substance requirement, Luxembourg’s CFC rules also contain specific exclusions. The CFC rule does not apply if a CFC has accounting profits equal to or less than EUR 750,000 or if its profit represents no more than 10% of its operating costs. These are the so-called de minimis thresholds under ATAD I.

In Luxembourg, CFC income is defined in Article 164ter LITL. CFC income consists of the non-distributed income of a controlled foreign company that arises from non-genuine arrangements put in place for the essential purpose of obtaining a tax advantage. An arrangement is considered non-genuine where the CFC would not own the assets or assume the risks generating the income were it not for the significant people functions carried out in Luxembourg by the controlling entity.
The income to be included under the CFC rule applies to amounts that are linked to those assets and risks connected with significant people functions performed in Luxembourg. In this way, categories such as interest, royalties, dividends, or other financial income may fall within scope only where they stem from non-genuine arrangements.

In Luxembourg, the CFC rules (Article 164ter LITL, implementing ATAD I Option B) include an exclusion for entities that carry out substantial economic activity. The assessment is based on whether the foreign entity has the people, assets, equipment and premises necessary to perform its functions and to assume the risks linked to its activities.
An arrangement is regarded as non-genuine where the CFC would not own the assets or bear the risks generating its income were it not for the significant people functions performed by the Luxembourg controlling company. Conversely, if the CFC itself employs staff, manages assets, and assumes risks through its own decision-making and operational capacity, its activities are considered genuine for purposes of the application of the CFC rule.

Under Luxembourg tax law, the trigger for applying the CFC rules is the “low-taxation condition” in Article 164ter LITL. The test is defined by reference to the Luxembourg domestic corporate income tax (CIT) rate. A foreign entity or permanent establishment qualifies as a CFC where its actual income tax liability is less than 50% of the Luxembourg CIT that would have been due on the same income.

Income subject to preferential tax regimes will be considered to be that which is not taxed abroad or is taxed at an income tax rate lower than 75% of the income tax that would be caused and paid in Mexico, in terms of Titles II (legal entities) or IV (individuals) of the Income Tax Law, as applicable.

Exclusions from CFCs:

• Income obtained by the taxpayer through a foreign tax transparent entity or foreign legal entity, regardless of whether it is subject to a preferential tax regime, when the taxpayer's indirect interest in said entity or legal entity is constituted by a structure that exclusively integrates one or more foreign tax transparent entities or foreign legal entities.

The foregoing applies to income obtained by the taxpayer through each of these entities or entities that comprise said structure.

Both cases mentioned above will be subject to the provisions of Article 4-B of the Income Tax Law.

• Income obtained through foreign entities that carry out business activities, unless their passive income represents more than 20% of their total income.

• The taxpayer must obtain authorization to exclude passive income generated by a foreign entity that is authorized to act as a financing entity by the authorities of the country in which they reside.

• When shares are sold within the same group, resulting from an international restructuring, provided they meet various requirements, including filing a notice with the tax authority prior to the restructuring.

It is a foreign entity subject to preferential tax regimes. Residents in Mexico and residents abroad with a permanent establishment in the country are required to pay tax on income subject to the regime that they obtain through foreign entities in which they participate, directly or indirectly, and exercise effective control over the foreign entity.

Article 176 defines when a foreign entity's income is subject to a preferential tax regime and establishes the criteria for effective control.
Effective control is considered to exist when any of the following conditions are met:

1. Average daily shareholding that grants:
More than 50% of the voting rights.
Veto right or favorable vote necessary for decisions.
More than 50% of the total value of the shares.

2. Right to assets or profits in the event of capital reduction or liquidation.
3. Sum of voting rights and asset rights exceeding 50%.
4. Consolidation of financial statements with the foreign entity.
5. Right to unilaterally determine decisions of meetings or management, including through an intermediary.

Furthermore, indirect effective control is considered if the taxpayer has control over intermediate entities that separate it from the final foreign entity.

The criteria for effective control are legal, economic, factual, and consolidation.

Income is generated in cash, goods, services, or credit by foreign entities, and income presumptively determined by the tax authorities, even if such income has not been distributed by such entities to taxpayers.

Passive income is considered to be: interest; dividends; royalties; gains from the sale of shares, securities, or intangible assets; gains from derivative financial transactions when the underlying asset relates to debt or shares; commissions and fees, as well as income from the sale of assets not physically located in the country or jurisdiction where the entity resides or is located; and income from services provided outside of said country or jurisdiction, or to persons not residing in said country or jurisdiction, as well as income from the sale of real estate, income from granting the temporary use or enjoyment of assets, and income received gratuitously.

There is a special treatment related to income from services provided to persons who do not reside in the country or jurisdiction where the foreign entity resides or is located.

In accordance with ATAD, the CFC regime does not apply to companies that mainly earn non-tainted income (i.e. the one third of income exception) or to financial institutions mainly receiving income from third parties (i.e. the one third of income exception for financial undertakings).

The CFC regime applies to the following types of income: a) interest or other benefits from financial assets; b) royalties or other benefits from intangible assets; c) dividends and capital gains derived from the disposal of shares; d) benefits from finance lease activities; e) benefits from insurance, bank or other financial activities; and f) invoicing activities from or to the taxpayer or related person, which add little or no economic value.

A CFC is defined as a company in which another company, alone or together with associated entities and/or persons, (i) owns directly or indirectly more than 50% of the capital, (ii) holds a direct or indirect participation of more than 50% of the voting rights or (iii) hold an entitlement to receive more than 50% of the profits.

The CFC regime applies to income generated by CFCs established in jurisdictions that (i) have a statutory corporate income tax rate of less than 9%, or (ii) are on the EU list of non-cooperative jurisdictions.

The genuine economic activity test is met if the CFC meets the Dutch minimum substance requirements, meaning, inter alia, that it must have its own office and incur employment costs of at least EUR 100,000 (which requirements originate from the Dividend withholding tax act 1965).

There are three tests:
1. a group of 5 or fewer New Zealand residents hold total interests in the company of more than 50%
2. a single New Zealand resident holds an interest of 40% or more unless at the same time a single non-resident holds an equal or greater interest
3. there is a group of 5 or fewer New Zealand residents who can control the exercise of the shareholder decision-making rights for the company
The CFC rules apply in all cases - there is no trigger rate.

"Attributable CFC amount" includes certain dividends, interest, royalties, rents, insurance income, income from supply of personal services, income from disposal of certain revenue account property, income from services physically performed in NZ, and certain income related to telecommunications services.

A CFC is not required to attribute income if its passive income is less than 5% of total gross income (CFCs in the same country can apply the 5% test at a consolidated level if certain conditions are met).

On the condition that Norway has signed a tax treaty with the country where the CFC is resident, and the foreign company in question is covered by the treaty, the CFC rules will be applicable only if the income of the entity in question is passive income.
CFC taxation do not apply if the foreign company is resident in a low-tax jurisdiction within the European Economic Area, and is not deemed as a wholly artificial arrangement.

The reference is 2/3 of  our domestic rate. Domestic CIT rate is currently 22%. Triggering rate: 14,67%.

Definition of Low-tax jurisdictions: Low-tax jurisdictions are jurisdictions in which the ordinary income tax on the overall profit of the company or undertaking is less than two thirds of the tax that would have been levied on such company or undertaking if it had been resident in Norway. The assessment include a comprehensive evaluation of the tax rules applicable to the specific type of entity in question. Considerations  include special tax regimes, differences in deduction rules, variations in depreciation rates, and tax incentives.

Control criteria:    1. There is deemed to be Norwegian control of a foreign company or undertaking if no less than one half of the ownership interests or capital of such company or undertaking are directly or indirectly owned or controlled by Norwegian taxpayers, at both the beginning and the end of the tax year.    2. There is also Norwegian control if the company or the undertaking were deemed to be Norwegian-controlled in the year before the tax year, unless less than one half of the ownership interests or capital are directly or indirectly controlled by Norwegian taxpayers, at both the beginning and the end of the tax year.    3. If Norwegian taxpayers own or control more than 60 percent of the ownership interests or capital as at the end of the tax year, there is Norwegian control irrespective of 1 and 2. Correspondingly, there is not Norwegian control if Norwegian taxpayers own or control less than 40 percent of the ownership interests or capital as at the end of the tax year.

Both active and passiv income. The Norwegian shareholders are taxed on their proportionate share of the entity's profits, calculated according to Norwegian tax rules. This involves:

2) Adjusting for differences in accounting and tax rules, and

The CFC tax regime affects taxpayers that are shareholders of foreign entities located (i.e. seated or having a place of management or being registered or situated) in: 
(I) countries recognised as applying harmful tax competition i.e., in the so-called tax havens  
or
(II) countries with which Poland/EU have not ratified any treaty (e.g. DTTs) allowing for exchange of tax information 
No other conditions have to be met in these cases for the foreign entity to be considered as a CFC.
In addition, a controlled foreign company (III) will be an entity that meets all of the following conditions:
the control level condition - Polish tax residents have directly/indirectly, solely or jointly with related entities or with non-related entities being Polish tax residents, over 50% participation in the foreign company s income, voting rights, or capital or exercise actual control over the foreign entity.
the level of taxation condition - Income tax actually paid by the foreign entity (not subject to refund or credit in any form, including the refund or credit for the benefit of another entity) is lower by at least 25% than the income tax that would be paid by this foreign company in Poland at the application of the 19% tax rate (if it was a Polish tax resident)
the revenue structure condition   at least 33% of the revenue of this entity earned in the tax year comes from the indicated sources (so-called passive income)
As of 2022. there are also 2 more categories of CFC entities regarding so-called "shell companies 
The first is entities (IV) that, in addition to meeting the level of control and the level of taxation conditions, have assets that generate passive income with a value equivalent to at least 50% of the value of the entity's total assets, and the passive income is less than 30% of the value of assets and receivables.
The last category of CFC (V) entities are those defined by reference to the rate of return on assets held. A foreign entity will be considered a CFC if, in addition to the level of control condition and the level of taxation condition, it earns income in excess of the income calculated according to the formula: (b + c + d)   20%, in which the various letters stand for: b - the carrying value of the entity's assets, c - the entity's annual employment costs, d - the accumulated (summed) previous depreciation and amortization within the meaning of the accounting regulations, and less than 75% of the entity's income is derived from transactions with unrelated parties domiciled, established, managed, registered or located in the same country as the entity.

(I) The Polish CFC rules do not apply to a non-resident company if the non-resident company is established and subject to tax on the worldwide income in a EU/EEA country, provided it meets the substantial real economic activity test. 
(II) In order to avoid double taxation (in the economic sense), a tax deduction has been introduced for the amount of income tax paid by a foreign controlled company in its country of residence. This deduction is made in the proportion in which the income of this company determined for the purposes of the CFC regulations (i.e., the income included in the tax base, after deducting the amounts of dividends received by the taxpayer from the foreign controlled entity and the amounts obtained from the taxpayer's disposal of its interest in the foreign controlled company for consideration) remains to the total income of this company. 
(III) Elimination of double or multiple income taxation on CFC income in cases of cascading dividends in holding structures

The Portuguese Controlled Foreign Company (CFC) Rule corresponds to Article 66 of the CIT Code.
This Article 66 was modified according the Directive (EU) 2016/1164 of 12 July 2016, laying down rules against tax avoidance practices that directly affect the functioning of the internal market (ATAD 1) [see Portuguese Law 32/2019, of 3 May].
According number 1 of the Article 66, the CFC regime applies to non-resident profit/income subjected to a clearly more favourable tax regime and if the Portuguese resident entity detains, directly or indirectly, at least 25% of the capital, of the voting rights or of the rights over the income or property elements of said non-resident entity.
This CFC regime is not applicable when the non-resident entity is resident or establish in another European Union Member State or in an Economic European Space Member State that is subject to the tax administrative cooperation equivalent to the one established at the European Union level and if the taxpayer demonstrates that the existence and operation of the entity correspond to valid economic reasons and it develops an economic activity of agriculture, commerce, industry or services, using people, equipment, assets and facilities.

The Portuguese CFC regime covers all types of profits/income included in the Portuguese CIT. 
But from this regime are excluded the non-resident entity were the income related to one or several of the following categories doesn’t represent more than 25% of the total income of the same non-resident entity: royalties or income of intellectual property, image rights or similar rights; dividends or income derived from capital disposal; leasing income; financial, insurance or factoring income related to operations with special related entities; interests or other capital income.
As said before, the trigger rate for the Portuguese CFC regime is a fixed one: 25%, or more, of the capital, of the voting rights or of the rights over the income or property elements.

CFC rules are triggered if the tax paid by the controlled foreign entity is less than half of the difference between the tax it would pay in Slovakia and the tax it would pay in its country of residence.

CFC rule not apply if one third or less of the income received by the controlled foreign company falls under the categories of income referred to in Q4.
The control test criteria are implemented in Article 67.h of the CITA-2, i.e., 50% direct or indirect participation in capital, voting rights, or profit.

1.	Interest or other income from financial assets
2.	Royalties or other income derived from intellectual property
3.	Dividends and income from the disposal of shares
4.	Income from financial leasing
5.	Income from insurance, banking, and other financial activities

The corporate income tax on profits actually paid by the entity is less than half of the corporate income tax that would be charged on such profits under CITA-2.

CFC rule not apply if, based on the facts and circumstances, the controlled foreign company carries out an economic activity for which it has personnel, equipment, assets, and premises at its disposal.

Other significant exemptions and exclusions under the Spanish CFC rules include:
•	De minimis rule: CFC income is not attributed if the passive income subject to the regime is lower than 15% of the foreign entity’s total income.

•	Participation exemption carve out: Dividends and capital gains derived from significant participations in active subsidiaries are generally excluded, aligning with Article 21 of the Spanish CIT Law.

•	Tax treaty and information exchange jurisdictions: When the CFC is resident in a jurisdiction with a tax treaty containing an effective exchange of information clause, only certain passive income is attributed.

•	Permanent establishment exclusion: Profits of a foreign permanent establishment that are already included in the Spanish tax base are not subject to the CFC rules.

Under Article 100(2) of the CIT Law, CFC income is not attributed when the foreign entity carries on a genuine business activity with adequate material and human resources, except for certain categories of passive income (such as financial, real estate, or certain intangible income).

This carve out ensures that the CFC rules mainly target entities lacking real economic substance.

A foreign entity is considered a Controlled Foreign Company (CFC) when the Spanish taxpayer, either alone or together with its associated enterprises, holds, directly or indirectly, at least 50 percent of capital, voting rights, or entitlement to profits of that entity. In addition, the effective corporate tax paid on its profits is lower than 75 percent of the corporate income tax that would have been payable under the Spanish corporate income tax regime.

As an additional condition, the CFC regime generally does not apply when the foreign entity carries on genuine economic activities supported by adequate personnel, assets, and premises.

CFC income generally includes passive income obtained by the foreign entity, such as dividends, interest, royalties, capital gains on shares or other securities, income from financial leasing and insurance activities, as well as income from the transfer of intellectual property rights.
In addition, income derived from related-party transactions involving goods and services without significant economic substance may also be subject to the CFC regime.

The Spanish CFC rules are triggered when the effective corporate income tax paid by the foreign entity is lower than 75% of the corporate income tax that would have been payable under the Spanish corporate income tax regime (general CIT rate: 25%).

This rule does not  establish  a fixed nominal trigger rate. However, in practice, the triggering rate is effectively 18.75% (i.e., 75% of 25%).

The rules contain a substance exclusion as from 1.1.2008, to be in line with the ECJs Cadbury judgment. This exemption from the general rule applies to income from a foreign legal entity that is resident within the European Economic Area (EEA), if the shareholder can prove that the foreign entity is established in the other country for business reasons and is engaged in real economic activities.

The CFC rules apply to resident companies and individuals, as well as any non-resident with a PE in Sweden, with an direct or indirect 25 % holding or control, by the taxpayer alone or together with associated persons, of capital or voting power in a foreign legal entity.

Under the general rule, the income of a controlled foreign entity is deemed to be subject to low taxation if it is not taxed at all or is subject to tax that is lower than 11,33 % (55% of the Swedish tax rate of 20,6 %. for income year 2024). However, income is not considered to be subject to low taxation if the foreign legal entity is a tax resident, and liable to income tax, in one of the countries listed in a white list, provided that the income in question has not been expressly excluded in the list. In addition, the CFC regime does not apply to income derived from a foreign legal entity engaged in international shipping activities, provided that also the shareholder is engaged in shipping activities, whether directly or indirectly through a legal person resident in the EEA.

For the companies participating in the capital of joint stock and limited liable companies whose legal and business headquarters are not located in Türkiye, participation profits of these companies obtained from these subsidiaries that meet the conditions listed in Article 5/1-b of Law No. 5520 are exempt from Corporate Income Tax.

Corporate income of foreign subsidiaries controlled by full fledged taxpayer real persons and institutions by holding at least 50% of their capital, dividend or voting right directly or indirectly, seperately or together, is subject to Corporate Income Tax in T rkiye whether distributed or not, if the conditions specified in Article 7 of Law No. 5520 (Corporate Income Tax) are met together.

Broadly speaking, a CFC charge arises  in respect of any trading profits where 50% of the relevant SPFs in relation to an asset or risk which generate those profits are carried out in the UK. For trading finance profits (banking and insurance) a charge will arise where the CFC is overcapitalised with funds received from UK connected persons (UK group companies). For non-trade finance profits, a charge will arise on profits relating to assets or risks attributable to UK SPFs , profits generated using UK connected capital (from UK group companies), arrangements in lieu of dividends to the UK and certain leasing arrangements. For  intra-group financing arrangements, a charge arises on profits if any of the related SPFs are in the UK, if the CFC is overcapitalised with funds from the UK, or if profits are otherwise diverted from the UK.  Entity level exemptions can apply in relation to low profits (de minimis threshold - less than  £50k profits in a 12 month period, or less than  £500k profits so long as passive interest income does not exceed  £50k in that period); low profit margins (where accounting profits are not more than 10% of relevant operating expenses); high effective tax rates (at least 75% of UK ETR) and excluded countries with similar tax base/rate to UK; subject to an anti-avoidance test and limits on passive income; Temporary exemption period for certain acquisitions, subject to anti-avoidance conditions;

UK CFC rules contain a specific tax exemption which applies where the local tax paid by the CFC is at least 75% of the tax that would have been paid under the UK corporation tax rules. So this is not a triggering rate as such, but rather a requirement that the local tax paid by the CFC is at least 75% of the CIT it would have paid in the UK.

UK CFC regime covers both active and passive income. It does not apply to capital gains. Charging provisions cover the following categories - profits from UK activities ; non-trade finance profits ; trading finance profits ; profits from captive insurance ; profits from solo consolidation arrangements ; profits from qualifying loan relationships (certain related party financing arrangements)

A foreign company is a CFC when UK persons, together with related persons in the UK or elsewhere, hold more than a 50% interest in that company, by reference to legal control, economic control, or accounting standards. A separate test applies to joint ventures. CFC income is computed on basis of UK corporate tax rules, with separate charging provisions for trading income, non-trade finance profits and trading finance profits.

The SPF approach in relation to trading profits and non-trade finance profits effectively applies a test of substance or relevant activity at an asset or risk level, which can be seen as a measure of relevant economic substance and activity.  For trading activity, where less than 50% of the profits relating to an asset or risk are attributable UK SPFs, such profits are exempt. For non-trade finance profits, an exemption will only apply if none of the relevant SPFs are carried out in the UK.  In addition, the rules apply a business premises condition in relation to trading profits and intra-group non-trading finance profits. Certain treatments can only apply if the business of the CFC is wholly or mainly carried on from premises in its territory of residence, to be occupied with a degree of permanence

A CFC is any foreign corporation if more than 50% of the total combined voting power of all classes of stock of such corporation entitled to vote or the total value of the stock of such corporation is owned directly or indirectly by United States shareholders (U.S. shareholder) on any day during the taxable year of such foreign corporation. A U.S. shareholder is defined as a United States person (U.S. person) who owns 10 percent or more of the vote or value of all classes of stock of a corporation. Constructive ownership rules can attribute foreign stock ownership of one person to a related person.

The United States has two sets of CFC inclusion rules.  A U.S. shareholder must include in income their share of the subpart F income (generally, passive/mobile income) of a CFC.  The subpart F income rules include a   de minimis rule   - income that would otherwise be subpart F income is not treated as subpart F income if it is less than the lesser of 5% of the CFC s gross income or USD $1,000,000.  However, all of a CFC s income will be treated as subpart F income if the CFC s subpart F income and insurance income exceeds 70% of the CFC s gross income.  The subpart F income rules also include a high tax exception   subpart F income that is subject to an effective rate of income tax imposed by a foreign country greater than 90% of the maximum rate of U.S. tax imposed on corporations (currently, greater than 18.9%).  The second set of rules (adopted in 2017) requires a U.S. shareholder to include in income their global intangible low-taxed income (GILTI).  The GILTI rules apply a formulaic approach which generally requires an income inclusion by the U.S. shareholder based on their share of the income of their CFCs after excluding a 10% return on tangible assets of the CFCs from the GILTI amount.  Such income also excludes income that is effectively connected to a trade or business in the United States (which is taxed separately), subpart F income, related-party dividends, foreign oil and gas extraction income, or income that would be subpart F but is excluded by the high-tax exception.  In addition, the GILTI regime has an exclusion for high-taxed income, pursuant to an election, similar to the high tax exception for the Subpart F rules.

As regards indirect ownership or control, it takes place when the Argentine resident controls the foreign entity through one of these means: (i) An entity which is controlled by or related to the Argentine resident; (ii) their spouse; (iii) their cohabitant; or (iv) Other taxpayers related by blood or marriage, in ascending, descending, or collateral lines, up to and including third-degree relatives.      
This requirement will be considered fulfilled, regardless of the percentage of ownership, when the Argentine resident, directly or indirectly, meets any of the following requirements with respect to foreign entities:
i) holds the right to dispose of the entity’s assets.
ii) has the right to elect the majority of the directors or managers and/or the Argentine resident takes part in the board of directors and has the votes to impose decisions.    
iii) has the votes to dismiss the directors or managers of the entity.    
iv) has a right to the entity’s profits.    
This requirement will also be considered fulfilled, regardless of the percentage of ownership, when at any time during the fiscal year at least 30% of the value of the assets of the foreign entity arises from financial investments that generate passive income from Argentine source considered exempt for foreign beneficiaries.
2) That the non-resident entity does not have the material and human resources necessary to perform its activity, or its income originates from: (i) passive income that represents at least 50% of the entity profits for the fiscal year, or (ii) income of any kind that directly or indirectly generates deductible expenses for related parties resident in Argentina.  In these last cases, only the results derived from this type of income shall be taxed in accordance with the provisions of this subsection.  
3) That the income or profits mentioned in section 2) above, are taxed at an effective rate that falls below 75% of the corporate tax rate at which they would have been taxed in Argentina. It is presumed that this condition is met if the foreign entity is constituted, domiciled, or located in a non-cooperative, low or no-tax jurisdiction or country.

The United States has two sets of CFC inclusion rules. A U.S. shareholder must include in income their share of the subpart F income (generally, passive/mobile income) of a CFC. The subpart F income rules include a de minimis rule - income that would otherwise be subpart F income is not treated as subpart F income if it is less than the lesser of 5% of the CFC’s gross income or USD $1,000,000. However, all of a CFC’s income will be treated as subpart F income if the CFC’s subpart F income and insurance income exceeds 70% of the CFC’s gross income. The subpart F income rules also include a high tax exception – subpart F income that is subject to an effective rate of income tax imposed by a foreign country greater than 90% of the maximum rate of U.S. tax imposed on corporations (currently, greater than 18.9%). The second set of rules (adopted in 2017) requires a U.S. shareholder to include in income their global intangible low-taxed income (GILTI). The GILTI rules apply a formulaic approach which generally requires an income inclusion by the U.S. shareholder based on their share of the income of their CFCs after excluding a 10% return on tangible assets of the CFCs from the GILTI amount. Such income also excludes income that is effectively connected to a trade or business in the United States (which is taxed separately), subpart F income, related-party dividends, foreign oil and gas extraction income, or income that would be subpart F but is excluded by the high-tax exception. Proposed rules would expand, pursuant to an election, the GILTI regime’s exclusion for high-taxed income to high taxed income that would not otherwise qualify as subpart F income.

Control criteria: 1. There is deemed to be Norwegian control of a foreign company or undertaking if no less than one half of the ownership interests or capital of such company or undertaking are directly or indirectly owned or controlled by Norwegian taxpayers, at both the beginning and the end of the tax year. 2. There is also Norwegian control if the company or the undertaking were deemed to be Norwegian-controlled in the year before the tax year, unless less than one half of the ownership interests or capital are directly or indirectly controlled by Norwegian taxpayers, at both the beginning and the end of the tax year. 3. If Norwegian taxpayers own or control more than 60 percent of the ownership interests or capital as at the end of the tax year, there is Norwegian control irrespective of 1 and 2. Correspondingly, there is not Norwegian control if Norwegian taxpayers own or control less than 40 percent of the ownership interests or capital as at the end of the tax year.  Low-tax jurisdictions: Low-tax jurisdictions are jurisdictions in which the ordinary income tax on the overall profit of the company or undertaking is less than two thirds of the tax that would have been levied on such company or undertaking if it had been resident in Norway. The Norwegian tax rate in 2018 is 23 pct.

In the case of the Polish CFC rules, in principle, control is not defined directly, but an indication of its meaning can be gleaned from the first (of three) conditions for constituting a CFC. The CFC rules refer to the 50 per cent control threshold and say that a Polish taxpayer controls a foreign company if he owns continuously for at least 30 days, directly or indirectly, at least (i) 50 per cent of the company’s capital (legal control); (ii) 50 per cent of the voting rights in the controlling or administrative organs of the company (legal control); or (iii) 50 per cent of the shares related to the right to participate in the company’s profits (economic control). Moreover, a foreign company whose tax residence is in one of the 26 tax havens is considered a CFC regardless of the level of control over this company, level of taxation of its profits, or type of income received by it (CFC presumption). The Polish CFC rules apply also to the foreign permanent establishment of a Polish taxpayer.

The control test is in line with the Article 7(1) of the EU Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive 2016/1164 (ATAD). The control test for a control foreign company is as follows [ITA Sec. 17h para 1 letter a)]: a corporate taxpayer (tax resident of the Slovak Republic) by itself, or together with its associated enterprises owns directly or indirectly more than 50% of the capital or holds a direct or indirect participation of more than 50% of the voting rights or is entitled to receive more than 50% of the profits of the foreign entity. Other condition, which has to be fulfilled is a tax rate test, i.e. the corporate tax paid by the controlled foreign company abroad is lower than the difference between the corporate tax of the controlled foreign company calculated under the Slovak Income Tax Act and the corporate tax paid by the controlled foreign company abroad [ITA Sec. 17h para 1 letter b)]. As the controlled foreign company is considered also the permanent establishment [ITA Sec. 17h para 3].

CFC rules are applied to the following entities:  1) A trust located abroad as long as the Argentine resident manage its assets. As examples of the existence of this management can be mentioned:   a) When the trust is revocable trust.  b) When the trustor and the trust’s beneficiary are the same person.  c) When the Argentine resident has the right to directly invest or the assets of the trust.  2) An entity which is not considered taxpayer in the foreign country, that is to say, its profits are directly assigned to the Argentine resident.  3) An entity which is considered taxpayer in the foreign country, as long as some requirements take place concurrently. These requirements are:  a) The Argentine resident control, directly or directly, the entity located in the other country. b) The non resident entity does not have the material and human resources to perform its activity or its passive and portfolio income are equal or greater than 50% of the entity profits, or its profits result on deductible expenses for related parties in Argentina. c) The income or profits mentioned in b) are taxed at a rate below than 75% of the rate at which those income or profits would have been taxed in Argentina, or the entity in question is located in a non-cooperative or low or no tax jurisdiction or country.  In order to determiner the condition mentioned in a), i.e. if the Argentine resident controls the entity located in other country, one of these cases has to take place:  a) The Argentine resident, directly or indirectly, owns 50% or more of the foreign entity net worth or profits. b) The Argentine resident, directly or indirectly, has 50% or more of the votes for taking decisions in the foreign entity. c) The Argentine resident, directly or indirectly, has the right to manage and sell the entity goods and properties. d) The Argentine resident, direct or indirectly, has the votes to appoint the board of directors of the entity. e) The Argentine resident takes part in the board of directors and has in it the votes to impose decisions. f) The Argentine resident, directly or indirectly, has the votes to dismiss the CEO or managers of the entity. g) The Argentine resident has any right on the entity profits. h) At least 30% of the value of the entity assets arises from financial investments that generate passive income from Argentine source. i) Passive and portfolio income obtained by the entity is taxed at a rate below than 75% of the rate at which those income would have been taxed in Argentina.  As regards indirect control, it takes place when the Argentine resident controls the foreign entity (i.e. one of the facts listened above takes place) through one of these means:  a) An entity which is controlled by the Argentine resident. b) Argentine resident’s relative (e.g.: spouse). c) The person who cohabits with the Argentine resident.

A controller that holds 20% or more of the voting capital of a company is deemed to have significant influence on this company.

An entity shall be treated as a controlled foreign company if the following conditions are cumulatively met: a) the taxpayer, alone or together with its associated enterprises, holds a direct or indirect holding of more than 50% of the voting rights or directly or indirectly owns more than 50% of the capital of the entity or is entitled to receive more than 50% of that entity's profits; b) the tax on profits actually paid for its profits by the entity or permanent establishment is less than the difference between the profit tax that would have been levied from the entity or the permanent establishment, calculated in accordance with the provisions regarding to the tax on profit from Fiscal Code of this Title and the profit tax actually paid for its profits by the entity or by the permanent establishment. For the purposes of this letter, the permanent establishment of an entity treated as a foreign controlled company shall not be taken into account in so far as the head office is not subject to taxation or is exempt from tax in the jurisdiction of the controlled foreign company.
